intro: Taekwondo is a Korean martial art famous for fast, high and spinning kicks. In Olympic sparring (kyorugi), athletes wear electronic trunk protectors and head-gear sensors that register valid hits, while judges award points for punches and technical elements. World Taekwondo (WT) publishes the Competition Rules.
inThirtySeconds: Score with kicks to the trunk protector and head, and punches to the trunk.
Harder techniques score more: a turning kick to the head is worth the most.
Contests are played over rounds; win two rounds to win the match.
Penalties (gam-jeom) give a point to the opponent.
objective: Win the majority of rounds by scoring more points than your opponent in each.

facts.duration: Best of three 2-minute rounds (senior international events)

scoring.label: Punch to trunk
scoring.detail: A straight punch to the trunk protector.

scoring.label: Turning kick to trunk
scoring.detail: Extra points for a valid spinning technique.

scoring.label: Kick to head
scoring.detail: Any valid kick to the head.

scoring.label: Gam-jeom
scoring.detail: Each penalty gives the opponent one point.

rules.title: Valid target areas
rules.summary: Kicks may target the trunk protector and the head above the collarbone; punches may only target the trunk.
rules.body: Attacks below the waist, punches to the head and attacks to the back of the head are not allowed. Kicks must use the foot below the ankle bone; knee strikes and hand strikes other than closed-fist punches are not permitted.

rules.title: Technique values
rules.summary: Trunk kicks score 2, head kicks 3, and valid turning (spinning) kicks earn extra points.
rules.body: Electronic sensors register trunk and head contact automatically; judges confirm punches and turning techniques with handheld scoring devices. Coaches may request video review of certain decisions.
rules.example: A spinning back kick lands on the head protector: 5 points.

rules.title: Win two rounds
rules.summary: Each round is won separately; the first athlete to win two rounds wins the match.
rules.body: If a round is tied on points, tie-break criteria apply, such as the athlete who scored more with higher-value techniques. A large enough points gap during a round ends that round early. Check the current WT Competition Rules for the exact thresholds, which have changed over recent cycles.

rules.title: Knockouts
rules.summary: If an athlete is knocked down by a legal technique and cannot continue after the referee's count, the opponent wins.
rules.body: The referee counts to eight when an athlete is knocked down, and may stop the contest if the athlete is unable to continue safely.

rules.title: Gam-jeom
rules.summary: Prohibited acts are penalised with a gam-jeom, which gives one point to the opponent.
rules.body: Common causes include crossing the boundary line, falling down, avoiding or delaying the match, grabbing or pushing the opponent, raising the knee to block or impede a kick, attacking below the waist, and hitting the opponent's head with the hand. Too many penalties lead to losing the match.

fouls.name: Crossing the boundary
fouls.description: Both feet leave the competition area.

fouls.name: Falling down
fouls.description: Any part of the body other than the feet touching the floor.

fouls.name: Grabbing or pushing
fouls.description: Holding the opponent or their kick.

fouls.name: Punching the head
fouls.description: Striking the face with the hand.

flow.title: Bow and start
flow.description: Athletes bow to each other; the referee signals 'Shi-jak' to start.

flow.title: Rounds
flow.description: Two-minute rounds with a rest in between.

flow.title: Result
flow.description: The referee raises the winner's hand.

positions.name: Hong (red)
positions.role: The other competitor wears red protectors.

field.name: Competition area
field.dimensions: Octagonal area, about 8 m across, inside a larger square
notes: Electronic scoreboard and video replay system at major events

glossary.definition: Forms — choreographed patterns judged for technique.
Penalty awarding a point to the opponent.
Protector and Scoring System — the electronic sensors.

funFacts: Taekwondo became a full Olympic sport at Sydney 2000.
Electronic scoring was introduced at the Olympics at London 2012.
